summary: The machine has the core tools and DocumentDB MCP/data-plane skills required to start building the sample pipeline (python, pip, node/npx, docker, az, the documentdb MCP server and many DocumentDB agent skills). Most of the model's cold answers were either partly wrong or outdated because they described Azure Cosmos DB (databaseAccounts / RU model / mongo API under Cosmos) or general MongoDB rather than the modern Azure DocumentDB product (resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters, vCore compute tiers, new vector APIs). Missing accelerators (DocumentDB Agent Kit) and a few CLI tools (mongosh, bicep, terraform, azd) would speed development but are not blocking; some operational choices (OpenAI model/dimensions, alert threshold, and seed-data) are not answered by installed skills and must be decided by the builder before coding.
summary_points: Core build tools for the sample are present: python/pip (3.13), node/npx, Docker, az (signed in), and the documentdb MCP server plus comprehensive DocumentDB skills.

Several cold answers were incorrect or outdated because they described Cosmos DB (databaseAccounts / RU model) or older connection/port conventions instead of Azure DocumentDB's current resource type (Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters), compute-tier billing (vCores/M-series), and connection URI form (mongodb+srv to *.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com).

Vector search uses cosmosSearch via createIndexes/createSearchIndexes with sub-kinds (vector-ivf, vector-hnsw, vector-diskann); the community-style createIndex(...) vector syntax is wrong for this service.
Important missing decisions the builder must make before coding: OpenAI embedding model & dims, anomaly threshold/metric, and a seed-data plan (scripts).

Useful accelerators are not installed (DocumentDB Agent Kit); mongosh is not on PATH and would help manual verification; missing IaC CLIs (bicep/terraform/azd) are helpful but not mandatory for this sample that uses an existing cluster.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB; primary resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (the Cosmos DB account resource).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB clusters are provisioned as Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (resource type 'mongoClusters'), not as Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. The correct resource type for this managed MongoDB-compatible cluster product is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cosmos DB's historical and API naming (Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts) for Cosmos DB accounts and older 'MongoDB under Cosmos' offerings overlap the provider namespace and the 'DocumentDB' name; a model that memorized Cosmos DB docs will state databaseAccounts.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder used Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts in IaC or az commands, they'd attempt to manage a different product (Cosmos account) and fail to create or manage the mongoClusters resource the sample must target.
improvements: Add a short deprecation/renaming note on the databaseAccounts docs explaining that the managed MongoDB vCore product is now represented by Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and link to the mongoClusters resource reference.
In the agent kit 'documentdb-azure-deployment' README add an explicit 'not Cosmos DB databaseAccounts' sentence to avoid misreading the provider.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the core CLI group az cosmosdb. Example to create: az cosmosdb create --name myAccount --resource-group myRG --kind MongoDB --locations regionName='eastus' --default-consistency-level Session
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB exposes az commands under the 'az documentdb mongocluster' command group (or az cosmosdb mongocluster in some aliasing); there is an 'az documentdb mongocluster create' command (documentdb is a distinct command group) and template-based deployment examples target Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters. Management of this product is via the 'documentdb'/'cosmosdb mongocluster' command group rather than the classic 'az cosmosdb create' account-level command for Cosmos databaseAccounts.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The older Cosmos 'databaseAccounts' CLI (az cosmosdb) is the natural match for many Mongo-related tasks in Cosmos; models trained on older Cosmos quickstarts produce that answer.
confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong CLI group (az cosmosdb create against databaseAccounts) could create a different type of resource (Cosmos account) that doesn't expose the mongoClusters vector features and would mismatch the sample's expectations.
improvements: Document the correct CLI command group in the sample README and the documentdb-azure-deployment skill (e.g., call out 'az documentdb mongocluster create' and show common examples).
Add a prominent note in 'az cosmosdb' docs linking to 'az documentdb' for vCore-based mongoClusters to reduce misdirection.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. Terraform (AzureRM provider): azurerm_cosmosdb_account (and azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_database / azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_collection for DB/collection resources).
confusions.grounded_answer: Bicep and Terraform templates for the current Azure DocumentDB product target Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (resource type 'mongoClusters'). Terraform's AzureRM provider exposes an 'azurerm_mongo_cluster' (or azapi/azurerm provider module) for this resource. Use the mongoClusters Bicep resource and the azurerm_mongo_cluster Terraform resource for vCore clusters.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The Terraform/Bicep resource names for Cosmos DB accounts (databaseAccounts/azurerm_cosmosdb_account) historically hosted MongoDB API variants; the vCore product uses distinct resource types and newer provider mappings.
confusions.build_risk: Using databaseAccounts/azurerm_cosmosdb_account types will provision a different resource family; IaC produced by the builder would not match the existing cluster and might be refused or create unintended resources.
improvements: Add a migration note on the 'databaseAccounts' and Terraform cosmos modules explaining the correct 'mongoClusters' resource for vCore-based DocumentDB, with code snippets.
Include a sample Bicep/Terraform fragment for `Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters` in the agent-kit templates.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Standard MongoDB URI form. Example: mongodb://myUser:myPassword@myaccount.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@myaccount@. Scheme: mongodb:// (tls required). Host suffix: *.mongo.cosmos.azure.com. Port: 10255 (TLS). Required options typically include ssl=true (or tls=true), replicaSet=globaldb and retryWrites=false.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB cluster connection strings use the SRV form and newer host suffixes. Example form: mongodb+srv://<user>:<password>@<cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?tls=true&authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256&retrywrites=false&maxIdleTimeMS=120000. The recommended scheme is mongodb+srv with host *.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com (or *.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com for single-cluster endpoints), use TLS (tls=true), and authMechanism commonly SCRAM-SHA-256 or MONGODB-OIDC for Entra-based auth; port 10255 is an older Cosmos convention and not the SRV modern form.

grounding_links.title: How to connect / quickstarts (connection string examples)
Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Python

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos DB for MongoDB examples used explicit hostnames and ports like 10255; the vCore DocumentDB product uses different endpoint hostnames (mongocluster) and favors SRV URIs and updated TLS/auth parameters.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder used the old mongodb:// + port form or incorrect host suffix, client connections would fail or attempt to talk to the wrong service; wrong auth options (e.g., leaving retryWrites default) may cause errors.
improvements: Add a 'connection string quick reference' snippet to the sample README showing the SRV form, recommended query options, and how to choose authMechanism (SCRAM vs MONGODB-OIDC).
Deprecate older docs that reference port 10255 for this product, or add a clear 'legacy Cosmos DB account connection strings' note linking to the new form.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Capacity is billed in Cosmos DB terms (Request Units / RU/s). You provision RU/s (or use autoscale/auto-provisioned RU/s or serverless where available). It is not billed purely by vCores for the MongoDB API (use RU/s or serverless autoscale options).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (the vCore DocumentDB product) is billed by compute tiers (vCore-style compute tiers: M10, M20, M30, ...), storage and optional features (not by request units / RU/s). The vCore model (compute tiers) is the correct billing model for this managed MongoDB-compatible product.

grounding_links.title: Why migrate to Azure DocumentDB / Overview (pricing mention)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The Cosmos DB family historically uses RU-based billing for its NoSQL and MongoDB serverless/throughput models; the vCore-based DocumentDB product uses compute tiers (M-series). The shared 'DocumentDB' / 'Cosmos DB' names cause model confusion.

confusion_sources.title: Cosmos DB databaseAccounts RU model docs

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumed RU/s billing, they may choose wrong tiering defaults, index/configuration and performance assumptions won't match the chosen cluster, and cost estimates would be wrong.
improvements: Explicitly call out the billing model on the product landing page and in 'documentdb-azure-deployment' (e.g., 'vCore compute tiers M10..M200; not RU/s').
Add a short guidance section explaining how to pick a compute tier for dev vs prod in the sample README.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: Primary data-plane auth is MongoDB username/password (SCRAM). Management-plane uses Azure AD. For Microsoft Entra ID authentication from a driver you must acquire an AAD access token (client credentials) and use that token in a supported mechanism (for management operations use Azure SDKs; for data-plane MongoDB drivers, standard SCRAM credentials are used — there is no generic MongoDB driver flow that directly accepts an AAD token).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports native SCRAM username/password credentials and Microsoft Entra ID for data-plane authentication. Drivers can use Entra/OIDC flows (authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC) or use SCRAM credentials; the product documentation describes authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC and examples for RBAC/Entra integration. Management operations still rely on Azure AD / control-plane credentials.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older practice (and many Cosmos docs) emphasize native SCRAM credentials; newer DocumentDB features add MONGODB-OIDC support for Entra-driven auth — a subtle but important advancement that a cold model can miss.

confusion_sources.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes only SCRAM and codes around environment-based passwords, they miss an option that allows managed identities and workload identity in Azure. Conversely, if they attempt a MONGODB-OIDC flow without the cluster supporting it or without appropriate tenant config, auth will fail.
improvements: Add an 'Auth options' section in the sample README showing both SCRAM connection-string examples and MONGODB-OIDC usage with references to portal steps for enabling Entra for data-plane.
In the developer skill docs, add a short example for using DefaultAzureCredential + OIDC for driver connections where applicable.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the official MongoDB drivers for your language (e.g., pymongo for Python). There is no separate MongoDB-specific client library for applications; do not use the Cosmos DB SQL SDK for MongoDB-compatible operations. For management you can use az CLI / Azure SDKs.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: applications should use standard MongoDB drivers (pymongo for Python, mongodb for Node, MongoDB drivers for other languages). There is no separate application-level SDK for Azure DocumentDB — the MongoDB wire protocol is supported by standard drivers. Management uses Azure CLI / provider SDKs.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Python

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: n/a
confusions.build_risk: Low — following this advice is correct.

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: Assuming a MongoDB-style vector index interface, supported index methods would be HNSW, IVF and DiskANN. Example createIndex command (Mongo shell style): db.activity_vectors.createIndex({ embedding: "vector" }, { dimensions: 1536, method: "hnsw", metric: "cosine", name: "embedding_hnsw_idx" })
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports vector sub-kinds: vector-diskann, vector-hnsw and vector-ivf. Index creation is performed via the createIndexes (server command) with key: { '<path>': 'cosmosSearch' } and additional cosmosSearchOptions specifying kind ('vector-ivf'|'vector-hnsw'|'vector-diskann'), dimensions, similarity, and algorithm-specific parameters (numLists, efConstruction, m, etc.). Example pattern: db.runCommand({ createIndexes: 'collection', indexes:[{ name:'idx', key:{'embedding':'cosmosSearch'}, cosmosSearchOptions:{ kind:'vector-ivf', numLists:1024, similarity:'COS', dimensions:1536 } }] })

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (createIndexes + cosmosSearch examples)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model proposed a MongoDB-native createIndex vector signature (common in some community extensions), but Azure DocumentDB uses the service-specific 'cosmosSearch' key and the createIndexes server command with cosmosSearchOptions.

confusion_sources.title: Example using an IVF index (shows createIndexes with cosmosSearchOptions)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder attempted to use db.createIndex({embedding:'vector'}) with driver-level index creation, the index would not be created in the expected vector engine and vector queries would fail or not be accelerated.
improvements: Add a small 'create vector index' snippet to the sample README using db.runCommand({createIndexes:...}) with cosmosSearchOptions for each supported kind.
In agent skills, prefer recommending the createIndexes pattern and include a copy-pasteable JSON template for IVF/HNSW/DiskANN.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Full-text search: create MongoDB text indexes with db.collection.createIndex({ field: 'text' }, { default_language: 'english' }) or integrate with Azure Cognitive Search for richer capabilities. Hybrid (vector + text) search is implemented in application code by combining a vector nearest-neighbour query (on the vector index) with a text filter or text-score post-filtering (execute vector NN then run text index queries or combine both results in application).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB provides a BM25 keyword search engine via createSearchIndexes (the new search engine) and the $search aggregation stage for keyword/BM25 queries. Hybrid search (lexical + vector) is supported server-side: you can create both a BM25 search index and a vector index on the same collection and combine them in a single aggregation pipeline (e.g., server-side Reciprocal Rank Fusion or $unionWith + $group) to fuse results. You do not rely on MongoDB text indexes for the richer BM25/hybrid scenarios; instead use createSearchIndexes + $search and the cosmosSearch vector operator.

grounding_links.title: Hybrid search (BM25 + vector) in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer fell back to classic MongoDB text indexes and external Azure Cognitive Search as a generic path; Azure DocumentDB has an integrated BM25 search and server-side hybrid fusion that is preferred for hybrid retrieval.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder used simple MongoDB text indexes and client-side fusion only, they'd miss server-side fusion benefits and the sample wouldn't demonstrate the product's integrated hybrid search capabilities.
improvements: Add a 'hybrid search' example pipeline in the sample demonstrating server-side fusion with $unionWith or RRF and reference the createSearchIndexes syntax for BM25 + cosmosSearch.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Typically Cosmos DB's MongoDB API supports a subset of MongoDB server versions (commonly older 3.6/4.0/4.2/4.4/5.0 families depending on account compatibility). Some advanced MongoDB server features are not supported or are limited: certain server-side JavaScript, mapReduce, some aggregation operators or pipeline stages, multi-document transactions (may be limited), and server modules not implemented in the compatibility layer. Expect to use the standard MongoDB drivers but avoid unsupported commands.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0 and aims to support the vast majority of MongoDB operators (documentation cites ~99.03% operator compatibility). Many aggregation operators and multi-document transactions are supported; the compatibility pages list exact supported/unavailable commands. The best practice is to consult 'MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility' for specifics.

grounding_links.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB
Azure DocumentDB at a glance (wire protocol versions supported)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer assumed older MongoDB compatibility limits (older v3.x/4.x) typical of Cosmos API pages; the modern Azure DocumentDB vCore product documents explicit support for 5.0-8.0 and much higher operator coverage.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder restricted themselves to old MongoDB syntax or avoided using newer operators, they'd unnecessarily degrade the sample and miss features; conversely, using an unsupported operator without checking compatibility could break at runtime.
improvements: Reference the exact compatibility table in the agent-kit docs and add a reminder in the sample README to run a quick compatibility check if migrating from another provider.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: For local development run a standard MongoDB server (Docker image mongo:latest) on port 27017. The Azure Cosmos DB Emulator does not reliably emulate the MongoDB API for all features, so prefer a local mongo server for driver testing. Example: docker run --rm -p 27017:27017 --name local-mongo -d mongo:7.0
confusions.grounded_answer: For local development the DocumentDB Gateway Docker image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest) is the recommended local deployment and exposes the MongoDB wire protocol on port 10260 (TLS + SCRAM-SHA-256). Using a plain mongo:latest is possible for some driver-level checks, but the gateway image yields closer parity (ports, TLS, extensions) with Azure DocumentDB features (vector/search behaviors).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: A generic model answer defaults to 'run mongo:latest on 27017' for local development. The DocumentDB project provides a specialized gateway image and a different port (10260) for feature parity (TLS cert handling and gateway behaviours).
confusions.build_risk: If the builder runs only a stock mongo container, they may miss TLS/enforcement, gateway-specific features (vector search), and index behaviors; tests may pass locally but fail against the live cluster.
improvements: Add a short local dev snippet to the sample README that shows the recommended Gateway Docker image and the correct port (10260) and explains TLS settings for local testing.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change streams support depends on the API/version: some MongoDB API versions expose change streams; where available you must use a supported wire-version/feature compatibility level on the account. If using Cosmos DB, you may instead use the Cosmos change feed for the SQL API. For MongoDB change streams, ensure your account is created with a MongoDB-compatible API version that advertises change stream support.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports change streams. For multishard clusters there is a gated preview that must be enabled in the cluster Features (Change streams for multishard clusters). Pre-images are optional and must be enabled per-collection. Normal (single cluster) change streams are supported; enabling multishard change streams requires turning off the Rebalancer and enabling the feature in portal.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer was cautious and generic; it omitted Product-specific enablement steps for multishard change streams in DocumentDB and portal feature flags.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder expects multishard change streams by default and doesn't enable the portal feature or follow the required prerequisites, their change-stream consumers will not receive cluster-wide events.
improvements: Add a short 'change streams' section in the sample README explaining when pre-images or multishard change streams must be enabled and linking to the portal steps.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the service-specific MCP server named documentdb (i.e., the documentdb MCP server). The general Azure MCP server does not include DocumentDB-specific data-plane tooling such as index introspection; use the documentdb MCP server for those features.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the documentdb MCP server provides DocumentDB data-plane tools (list indexes, create indexes, run aggregations) and is separate from the general Azure MCP server. The installed machine inventory shows the 'documentdb' MCP server is available and contains the appropriate data-plane tools.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: n/a
confusions.build_risk: None — the inventory confirms the documentdb MCP server exists.

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Azure DocumentDB was the original name for Microsoft's managed JSON document DB service; it was later rebranded as Azure Cosmos DB. The Azure "DocumentDB" name historically refers to the precursor of Cosmos DB. The open-source project named DocumentDB is unrelated; Azure's DocumentDB/Cosmos DB is a proprietary Microsoft service exposing multiple APIs (SQL, MongoDB-compatible, Cassandra, Gremlin, Table).
confusions.grounded_answer: This is a common source of confusion. The product in this sample is 'Azure DocumentDB' (Microsoft's managed MongoDB-compatible product) — it is distinct from the legacy 'Azure DocumentDB' product that was rebranded into Azure Cosmos DB long ago. The current vCore MongoDB-compatible offering was previously referred to in some contexts as 'Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)', but the product team now exposes it as Azure DocumentDB (backed by the open-source DocumentDB engine). The open-source DocumentDB engine (github.com/documentdb/documentdb) is the engine project that implements the server; it is related (the managed service runs that engine) — not an unrelated project.

grounding_links.title: Moving from another MongoDB-compatible service to Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Product names have evolved (DocumentDB → Cosmos DB → Cosmos DB for MongoDB vCore → DocumentDB) and some docs still reference legacy names; the model conflated historical and current names.

confusion_sources.title: Compare & migration docs that mention 'vCore' and older names

confusions.build_risk: Naming confusion could lead to incorrect marketing text or IaC targeting the wrong API; code that assumes a Cosmos DB databaseAccounts resource may fail to match the existing cluster.
improvements: Add an 'About the name' short paragraph in the sample README clarifying 'Azure DocumentDB (vCore, Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters) — not Cosmos DB databaseAccounts' and link to the open-source engine repo.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Underneath the MongoDB-compatible API is the Cosmos DB engine (a protocol translation layer), not a stock mongod process. Application code should use standard MongoDB drivers, but must avoid server features not implemented by the compatibility layer and be mindful of differences in consistency, transaction and indexing semantics.
confusions.grounded_answer: The Azure DocumentDB product in this sample runs on the open-source DocumentDB engine (the microsoft/documentdb project) rather than being a simple protocol translation over Cosmos DB engine; however it exposes the MongoDB wire protocol so standard MongoDB drivers work in application code. The practical guidance stands: use MongoDB drivers and validate feature compatibility (but the underlying engine is DocumentDB, not Cosmos DB internal only).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer conflated the Cosmos DB implementation with this vCore DocumentDB product; both live under Microsoft and share namespaces historically, but the engine here is DocumentDB (open-source).

confusion_sources.title: Compare page that clarifies engine and compatibility

confusions.build_risk: If a builder assumes the underlying engine is Cosmos DB (SQL engine), they may expect features or behaviors that differ from DocumentDB's engine; however application-level code using standard MongoDB drivers will generally be compatible.
improvements: Add an explicit 'engine' line in the product overview and sample README making the relationship (open-source DocumentDB engine) clear.

confusions.question: What index definition does this sample need for vector search?
confusions.cold_answer: Create a vector index on the embedding field. Example (Mongo shell style): db.employee_vectors.createIndex({ embedding: "vector" }, { name: "embedding_ivf_idx", dimensions: 1536, method: "ivf", metric: "cosine", nlist: 1024 }) — adjust dimensions to the model output size.
confusions.grounded_answer: Create a vector index via the server 'createIndexes' command using key: { '<path>': 'cosmosSearch' } and cosmosSearchOptions specifying kind:'vector-ivf' (or 'vector-hnsw'/'vector-diskann'), dimensions, similarity (COS/L2/IP) and algorithm-specific params (numLists/nProbes, efConstruction, m, etc.). Example: db.runCommand({ createIndexes: 'employee_vectors', indexes:[{ name:'embedding_ivf_idx', key:{'embedding':'cosmosSearch'}, cosmosSearchOptions:{ kind:'vector-ivf', numLists:1024, similarity:'COS', dimensions:1536 } }] })

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (IVF example)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold example used a generic createIndex vector syntax; DocumentDB uses the cosmosSearch key and createIndexes server command with cosmosSearchOptions.
confusions.build_risk: Using incorrect index creation commands will leave documents unindexed for vector search and make similarity queries slow or incorrect.
improvements: Provide an explicit createIndexes template in the sample repository for vector-ivf/hnsw/diskann with recommended default parameters for small/medium demo datasets.

confusions.question: How do you compute an employee historical centroid in an aggregation pipeline?
confusions.cold_answer: Aggregate by employeeId, accumulate the embeddings into a running sum and count, then divide sums by count. Example conceptual pipeline using $reduce/$map and $arrayElemAt.
confusions.grounded_answer: This approach is supported: use $group to sum element-wise embeddings and $sum to get counts, then $project computing centroid as element-wise division using $map, $range, $arrayElemAt and $divide (or use $reduce to accumulate vectors). Azure DocumentDB supports $reduce, $map and array-expression operators needed for element-wise aggregation.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: n/a
confusions.build_risk: Low — ensure embeddings are stored as fixed-dimension number[] and avoid documents with missing or null vectors (handle in pipeline).
improvements: Add a tested aggregation pipeline snippet in the sample showing an $group + $project centroid computation to remove friction for builders.

confusions.question: How should embeddings be stored in documents?
confusions.cold_answer: Store embeddings as an array of doubles under a consistent field name, e.g. embedding: [0.0123, -0.234, ...]. Use a field type that the vector index expects (array of doubles) and keep a fixed dimensionality for all documents.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: vectors must be stored as a number[] (e.g., array of doubles) under a consistent field, and all documents indexed must use a fixed dimensionality. The vector-search docs explicitly state vectors must be number[].

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: n/a
confusions.build_risk: Low if followed; mismatch in dimensions or wrong type will cause the document to be unindexed.

confusions.question: What does the nearest-neighbour query for an embedding look like against the DocumentDB vector index in the sample?
confusions.cold_answer: Use a provider-specific vector search operator. Example Mongo-style call: db.employee_vectors.find({ $vectorSearch: { field: "embedding", query: [/*embedding*/], k: 10, metric: "cosine" } })
confusions.grounded_answer: Use the $search aggregation stage with the 'cosmosSearch' operator. Example: { $search: { cosmosSearch: { vector: <query_vector>, path: 'embedding', k: 10 } } } and use $project with {$meta: 'searchScore'} to get the similarity score. The $vectorSearch name is not the operator; use cosmosSearch within $search.

grounding_links.title: Vector search with cosmosSearch in $search aggregation stage

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold shape resembled some other vector-search syntaxes (community $vectorSearch) or driver helper libraries; Azure DocumentDB uses 'cosmosSearch' inside $search.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder attempts a non-supported operator name at the driver, the query will fail; must use $search + cosmosSearch syntax.
improvements: Include concise example $search + cosmosSearch snippet in the sample README and the codebase tests.

confusions.question: What auth flow will the pipeline use to read from DocumentDB and call OpenAI embeddings?
confusions.cold_answer: Use a service principal (Azure AD app) for DocumentDB management/inspection and a MongoDB user credential for the data-plane driver. Provision a dedicated MongoDB user with password on the sample_banking_19 database and put the connection URI in DOCUMENTDB_URI env var. For OpenAI embeddings, store OPENAI_API_KEY in env. For automation (nightly job) use a service principal for management tasks and keep data-plane credentials in environment variables/secrets.
confusions.grounded_answer: Reasonable and pragmatic: for the sample the simplest path is a native MongoDB user credential embedded in DOCUMENTDB_URI (read from env var) for the data-plane pipeline, and OPENAI_API_KEY from env for embeddings. Optionally, for managed Azure authentication, the cluster supports MONGODB-OIDC (Entra) so you can use DefaultAzureCredential (workload identity) for automation; management/portal ops still use Azure AD/service principal. The sample should document both choices and demonstrate the env-var pattern for reproducibility.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID (authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer is practical but omits the alternate Entra OIDC flow which the product supports; it's not wrong but incomplete.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder picks only one flow, they must ensure secrets/rotation are handled; for a sample using env vars is acceptable but must highlight security concerns.
improvements: Document both options in the sample README: (A) simplest: DOCUMENTDB_URI with MongoDB user; (B) managed: MONGODB-OIDC + DefaultAzureCredential, and links showing how to enable it.

information_gaps.title: OpenAI embedding model & dimensionality
information_gaps.description: No installed skill or docs specify which OpenAI embedding model the sample should use (text-embedding-3-small, text-embedding-3-large, etc.), which determines embedding dimensionality (e.g., 1536). I inspected Microsoft Learn and the DocumentDB skills but found no opinionated choice for this sample. The builder must pick a model and record its dimensionality (and update the index 'dimensions' accordingly).

information_gaps.title: Anomaly threshold definition
information_gaps.description: The prompt requires 'flagging significant deviations' but there is no prescribed similarity/distance threshold or detection algorithm (cosine similarity cutoff, statistical z-score, or learned classifier). No skill answered this; the builder must pick and document the threshold and metric and how it was chosen (example: cosine < 0.7 or Mahalanobis distance > X).

information_gaps.title: Seed/sample-data specification
information_gaps.description: The run environment assumes activity logs exist but provides no seed dataset or schema. No installed skill provided a specific seed script for 'sample_banking_19'. The builder needs to create an idempotent seed script and define realistic event types/fields and volume (e.g., 50–200 employees).

information_gaps.title: Nightly job orchestration preferences
information_gaps.description: The prompt requests a nightly job but does not say whether to use cron, Azure Functions, Azure Container Instances, or a simple scheduled runner. No specific CI/CD or scheduling guidance is present in the installed skills for this sample; the builder must pick an approach and document it. (azd or bicep presence would help if provisioning a schedule in Azure.)

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use the resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters for any IaC or Azure CLI commands that target the DocumentDB cluster; do not attempt to manage this cluster via Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts.

Create vector indexes with the service-specific createIndexes (runCommand) pattern using key: { '<path>': 'cosmosSearch' } and cosmosSearchOptions (kind: 'vector-ivf'|'vector-hnsw'|'vector-diskann', dimensions, similarity, and algorithm params); do not use a generic db.createIndex(... {method:'hnsw'}) call.

sources.title: Vector search: example using an IVF index

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use mongodb+srv SRV-style connection strings that point to <cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com with tls=true and authMechanism set appropriately (SCRAM-SHA-256 for native users or MONGODB-OIDC for Entra OIDC); do not rely on legacy ports like 10255.

inventory_recommendations.name: azd
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this sample (the run environment provides an existing cluster). Install azd only if you want azd-driven full-stack deployment demos; otherwise document using az + Bicep scripts. To add: install Azure Developer CLI (azd) from Microsoft Learn.

inventory_recommendations.name: bicep
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Helpful for authoring and validating the provided Bicep templates locally. Install the bicep CLI (dotnet / winget / manual) or use 'az deployment group create --template-file' which supports Bicep; document this fallback in README.

inventory_recommendations.name: terraform
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Useful only if the project aims to ship Terraform examples. Not required for the sample that targets an existing cluster. If desired, install Terraform and use the AzAPI/azurerm provider with azurerm_mongo_cluster module.

inventory_recommendations.name: dotnet
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not needed for the Python sample; only add if adding .NET sample variants or using Azure Functions .NET triggers in demos.

inventory_recommendations.name: mongosh
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Install mongosh to enable fast manual verification (connect via SRV URI, test $search and listIndexes). If unavailable, use the documentdb MCP server tools or small Python 'pymongo' scripts to run the same checks.
